blocks.text: That the raven is an animal fond of solitude is generally agreed. Accordingly Hesychius has: Σκορακίζει· εἰς ἔρημον πέμπει, καὶ ἀρᾶται, ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰς κόρακας πέμπειν [Skorakizei; eis erēmon pempei, kai aratai, apo tou eis korakas pempein]. The sense is that to send to the ravens is the same as to curse someone, wishing that he be banished and relegated to the wilderness. Of the same kind is the remark of the Scholiast on Aristophanes in the Clouds, on the proverb Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρ κας [Ball᾽ es kor kas], that ravens ἐν τοῖς ἐρημοτέροις τόποις ἐπιτηρεῖν τὰ σώματα [en tois erēmoterois topois epitērein ta sōmata], watch for corpses in solitary places. Here too [II, 790] belongs the prediction in Es. XXXIV, 10, that after Idumaea has been laid waste, the owl and the raven will dwell in the ruins of its metropolis Bosra. To this is added Sophon. II, 14, on the devastation of Nineveh: The voice of one singing in the window, the raven on the lintel. For so Jerome has it. And the version of the Greeks: Θηρία φωνήσει ἐν τοῖς διορύγμασιν αὐτῶν, καὶ κόρακες ἐν τοῖς πυλῶσιν αὐτῆς [Thēria phōnēsei en tois diorygmasin autōn, kai korakes en tois pylōsin autēs]; Beasts will cry out in their (the Ninevites') ditches, and ravens in her gates (Nineveh's). And Theodoret, on this passage, counts among the signs of devastation κοράκων νεοττίαι [korakōn neottiai], nests of ravens. And Cyril understands by the ravens night-ravens, which would not dwell in the very gates of the city unless there were a great deal of quiet and leisure there, which is most agreeable to their nature: Οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἐμφιλοχωρήσειαν αὐτοῖς πυλῶσιν οἱ νυκτικόρακες, εἰ μὴ πλείστη τις ὅση καὶ ἁνδάνουσα λίαν τοῖς ὧδε φύσεως ἔχουσιν ὑπάρχῃ σχολή [Oud᾽ an emphilochōrēseian autois pylōsin hoi nyktikorakes, ei mē pleistē tis hosē kai handanousa lian tois hōde physeōs echousin hyparchē scholē]. But the Hebrew word חרב choreb, which they explain as raven ^{(1)}, means dryness and devastation; or, if you read chereb, sword. Accordingly the Syriac translator renders it sword, as does Aquila too. And others among the Greeks render it dryness, as Jerome attests; why he preferred to render it raven, I cannot grasp at all. In the Hebrew (he says) is written חרב, which, according to the difference of reading, is taken as either dryness, or sword, or raven. As if חרב with Cheth and ערב with Ajin were the same. No one would grant Jerome that. For ערב, with Ajin and Cholem, means raven; but חרב, with Cheth and Cholem, means dryness and devastation, or sword if it has Segol. Since here, then, they write חרב with Cheth and Cholem, the words of Zephaniah are to be rendered thus: A voice will resound from the window; devastation will be on the threshold, when the cedar has been laid bare, that is, the cedar panelling. By voice here I understand one such as in Es. XIII, 21.

Here it may be asked why Solomon calls ravens ערבי נחל, ravens of the valley, or, if you prefer, ravens of the torrent, Prov. XXX, 17. For נחל means both valley and torrent ^{(2)}. I would take it as ravens of the valley, with the Greeks, who have κόρακες ἐκ τῶν φαράγγων [korakes ek tōn pharangōn], that is, ravens from the valleys, or those that like to nest in secluded valleys, which in Hebrew you might rightly call נחלי הבתות, valleys of the wastes [II, 791], with the Prophet Es. VII, 19. One may also understand some particular valley frequented by ravens and named after them. Isaiah could be understood of some such valley, were it not for the Masoretes, when he says of the riches of the Moabites, Es. XV, 7: על נחל הערבים ישאום, that is, as it is commonly rendered, They will carry them to the valley of the Arabs, or to the torrent of willows. And that indeed rightly, since the vowels supplied by the Masoretes [col. 201] do not allow us to interpret otherwise. But if they were absent, one could just as well read, They will carry them to the valley of the ravens. In this sense it is said in Greek Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρακας [Ball᾽ es korakas], that is, εἰς ἀπώλειαν, καὶ εἰς φθοράν [eis apōleian, kai eis phthoran]. And in Isaiah himself, II, 20, to cast idols to the moles and the bats is to destroy and cut them off. Now, if one may indulge in conjecture, that valley of the ravens was the very one that is called the valley of corpses in Ierem. XXXI, 40. And the same valley was called by both names because ravens, flocking together from every side, consumed the corpses of the condemned thrown into it. Granting this, when Solomon says that the ravens of the valley will pick out the eye that mocks its father, it will be as if he had said that one guilty of so foul a crime, having suffered an infamous punishment, is to be thrown into the valley of corpses, to be consumed there by ravens. For it counts as part of the penalty for the guilty that their corpses lie unburied or hang, to be torn apart by wild beasts or by carnivorous birds. Hence in Aristophanes' Θεσμοφορούσαις [Thesmophorousais] Mnesilochus begs to be spared punishment on this account, that he, an old man, should not be laughed at by the women τοῖς κόραξιν ἑστιῶν [tois koraxin hestiōn], providing a banquet for ravens. And shortly after, Ἐκρέμασε κόραξι δεῖπνον [Ekremase koraxi deipnon], He hung him up, to be a dinner for ravens. Horace too, Epistle 16 to Quintius,
— — — you will not feed the ravens on the cross:
